doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

chapter: Vibes, Bermuda and arriving in Canada
title: Bound for Bermuda: seeing Lionel Hampton at Bop City and discovering vibes
summary: On a flight stopover at Christmas 1949 he heard Hampton at Bop City; Hampton and Red Norvo's records had inspired him to play vibraphone.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Okay. Well I wanted to ask you, I read this little anecdote. I guess you were en route from Bermuda to Canada or something and you had a stop in New York?
It was going to Bermuda, from England.
And you happened to see Lionel Hampton?

Yes. We flew over on BOAC and we got behind. And consequently they put us up at the Gotham Hotel, 55th and Fifth Avenue. They don’t do that anymore. And I had never been to North America. All I could remember in my lifetime is rationing, you couldn’t buy clothes, couldn’t buy candies, you only got an ounce and a quarter of meat a week or something or other, it was pretty bad. And when I got this offer from the same chap, I say, “Oh boy, you play the bloody drums?” He wrote me this letter, because we didn’t have a telephone, we couldn’t get a telephone during the war. “Would you be interested in an 18-month contract in Bermuda, with the possibility of a stay over in New York?” I said, “Oh my God, yeah.” So anyway we get to New York and they ushered us down into the Gotham, which was at 55th and Fifth Avenue, not bad. And we only had $25 between us, because of the currency restrictions. I think we had $5 each. In those days it was very difficult. The war had just finished and, it was finished a couple of years, it was Christmas 1949. So we walked down 55th toward Broadway, not knowing where we were going, and I see this sign, “Bop City.” Doug Duke at the organ, the George Shearing Quintet, and Lionel Hampton and his Orchestra. I said, “Guys we’ve got to go in.” They said, “We don’t have the money.” “Well let’s see how much it is.” I think it was two bucks to go in. Anyway we all went in and I heard him play that night. I had seen him on the movies before, you know. He’d been my inspiration in England. He was the only vibraphone player I was aware of, until 1946, when I was walking through a Woolworth’s Store and I heard this Benny Goodman record of “Slipped Disc.” And it was Red Norvo with Slam Stewart and that wonderful group. So that was it. And I went back to Bermuda and once I got enough money together I took a vacation up in New York and I bought a larger vibraphone because mine was very tiny. Actually I’ll tell you this very brief story about the vibraphone and how I got attached to it. During the war I used to go out and entertain the troops at various stations.
